summary: The note is an incident report on the September 15, 2023 storm-related power outage that disrupted the Bay City transit system. It covers the initial chaos, how the outage spread across connected services, the communications response, community and inter-agency support, and the resulting plans for weatherproofing, drills, smart grid funding and electric buses. It frames the outage as a lesson in preparedness and resilience.
one_line: Report on the September 15, 2023 Bay City storm power outage that disrupted transit, and the response and resilience measures that followed.
key_facts: On September 15, 2023, a massive power outage following a severe storm system disrupted the Bay City transit system.
The storm knocked out multiple substations in the early morning hours.
Nurse Maria O'Connor's usual 40-minute transit ride to the city hospital became a two-hour ordeal involving partially powered trains and overcrowded buses.
Information flow was patchy at first because of overlapping infrastructural failures.
The outage affected trains, trams, traffic lights, airport shuttles and ride-sharing scheduling systems.
By midday, Robert Dillard, Bay City's Chief of Transportation, announced that substantial sections of the system were limited or shut down entirely.
By late afternoon, officials had a communications strategy using text messages, social media, local media and digital signage on backup power.
Authorities stressed the need for multiple, redundant channels of information dissemination during outages.
Taxi companies adhered to a city-mandated cap on surge pricing, and local businesses near stations stayed open late.
Pastor Elizabeth King led volunteers who set up temporary shelters and distributed food and water.
Extra buses were marshaled from neighboring cities to cover the most critical routes.
City engineers proposed more robust weatherproofing near key power lines serving transportation nodes.
Transit authorities began drills and simulations to speed action plans and tighten coordination with emergency services.
The city's transit committee decided to apply for federal grants for smart grid technology to isolate failures and limit the spread of outages.
Electric buses with onboard batteries able to run independently of the grid became a priority, promoted by councilperson Jamal Richardson.
